name: Botswana
summary_text: Consensual same-sex conduct is legal in Botswana. Both male and female same-sex acts became legal on 11 June 2019 through a unanimous High Court ruling in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General declaring Penal Code Section 164 unconstitutional. The Government appealed in July 2019. The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the appeal on 29 November 2021, holding that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." Paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164 were formally deleted from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026.  Before June 2019, custody exposure rested on Section 164(a) and (c). The provisions criminalised sodomy, whether heterosexual or homosexual, and applied to both men and women. The maximum penalty was seven years' imprisonment.  Prosecution was rare while the offence stood. The United States State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found police "did not target same-sex activity" that year. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would lose him an election.  One criminal provision remains formally unresolved in the sources. At the United Nations Universal Periodic Review 43rd session in May 2023, Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendation to repeal Penal Code Section 167 concerning same-sex conduct between women.  Transgender people have a constitutional right to change their legal gender, established through court orders rather than an administrative procedure. In September 2017 the High Court held that refusal by the Registrar of National Registration to change a transgender man's gender marker was unreasonable and violated constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government initially announced it would appeal but decided against it in December and supplied the man with a new identity document reflecting his gender identity. In December 2017 the High Court ruled in a parallel case that the Government must recognise activist and transgender woman Tshepo Ricki Kgositau's gender identity. Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle following gender confirmation surgery in December 2016 and dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." The trans legal-gender right was confirmed through 2017 to 2022.  No clear administrative process for legal gender recognition exists for a visitor to rely on. The May 2023 Universal Periodic Review record states that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced" and Botswana did not accept the recommendation to introduce one.  In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation. Legal commentator Carmel Rickard assessed that this gives LGBTQ Batswana an even stronger, constitutionally based argument against discrimination.  Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Botswana in the form of marriage or civil unions.  The recorded baseline for violence was low in the year surveyed, alongside documented societal discrimination. The 2011 United States State Department report found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year and separately recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people. A regional tolerance survey found the share welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour rose from 43 percent in 2016 to 50 percent in 2021.  Official signals are mixed. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. In September 2016 President Ian Khama deported anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists called the Government's 2019 appeal an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia. In May 2024 the Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed that implementation of the association, gender-marker and decriminalisation precedents across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far."  A functioning, legally registered community infrastructure exists. The Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO in 2016 on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds. LEGABIBO operates as Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, including a World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong, with Coming Out, Law and Constitution and Help and Support resources.

The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the appeal on 29 November 2021, holding that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." Paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164 were formally deleted from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026.  Before June 2019, custody exposure rested on Section 164(a) and (c). The provisions criminalised sodomy, whether heterosexual or homosexual, and applied to both men and women. The maximum penalty was seven years' imprisonment.  Prosecution was rare while the offence stood. The United States State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found police "did not target same-sex activity" that year. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would lose him an election.  One criminal provision remains formally unresolved in the sources. At the United Nations Universal Periodic Review 43rd session in May 2023, Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendation to repeal Penal Code Section 167 concerning same-sex conduct between women.  Transgender people have a constitutional right to change their legal gender, established through court orders rather than an administrative procedure. In September 2017 the High Court held that refusal by the Registrar of National Registration to change a transgender man's gender marker was unreasonable and violated constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government initially announced it would appeal but decided against it in December and supplied the man with a new identity document reflecting his gender identity. In December 2017 the High Court ruled in a parallel case that the Government must recognise activist and transgender woman Tshepo Ricki Kgositau's gender identity. Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle following gender confirmation surgery in December 2016 and dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." The trans legal-gender right was confirmed through 2017 to 2022.  No clear administrative process for legal gender recognition exists for a visitor to rely on. The May 2023 Universal Periodic Review record states that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced" and Botswana did not accept the recommendation to introduce one.  In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation. Legal commentator Carmel Rickard assessed that this gives LGBTQ Batswana an even stronger, constitutionally based argument against discrimination.  Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Botswana in the form of marriage or civil unions.  The recorded baseline for violence was low in the year surveyed, alongside documented societal discrimination. The 2011 United States State Department report found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year and separately recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people. A regional tolerance survey found the share welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour rose from 43 percent in 2016 to 50 percent in 2021.  Official signals are mixed. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. In September 2016 President Ian Khama deported anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists called the Government's 2019 appeal an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia. In May 2024 the Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed that implementation of the association, gender-marker and decriminalisation precedents across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far."  A functioning, legally registered community infrastructure exists. The Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO in 2016 on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds. LEGABIBO operates as Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, including a World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong, with Coming Out, Law and Constitution and Help and Support resources.
